Before you beginPast eventYesterday, I walked to school.“Walked” presents the walk as a past event.Current routineI walk to school on most school days.“Walk” describes a current habit. It does not mean I must be walking at this exact moment.Future planTomorrow, I will walk to school.“Will walk” presents the walk as a future action. Use the base verb after “will”: will walk, not will walked.All three sentences keep the walker and destination. The verb groups and time context change how the reader places the event in time. You can write about an imagined journey; no journey is required.Read the Topic Guide · Open Classroom View

Before you beginAva said, “We should leave now.” The speech tag comes first, followed by a comma. With the tag last, write: “We should leave now,” Ava said. The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark; the full stop ends the sentence after said.Use paper or your usual writing support. If listening to a question, also inspect the written options or ask an adult to name the punctuation marks exactly: a spoken reading alone may not reveal which marks are printed. A student can dictate punctuation and paragraph breaks; the adult checks the actual recorded writing.Read the Topic Guide · Open Classroom View
